summary: Defines Shim6, a layer 3 shim that provides locator agility below the transport protocols. It gives IPv6 multihoming with failover and load sharing, without needing a site to have provider-independent address prefixes in the global routing system.

eli5.summary: A site connected through two providers has two addresses. This note adds a layer that lets conversations switch between them if one fails.

subtitle: A host-based layer that lets IPv6 conversations switch to another address when a provider link fails, without a provider-independent prefix.

tldr.problem: A site with several IPv6 provider-allocated prefixes wants established communication to survive an outage on one connection, without a provider-independent prefix announced in the global routing table.
tldr.mechanism: Hosts set up a ULID-pair context with a peer using a four-message exchange. When the working address pair fails, a shim layer below the transport protocols swaps in another locator pair and tags packets with a Context Tag so the receiver can restore the original addresses.
tldr.outcome: Upper layers keep seeing the same addresses while packets travel over different paths. The work is done in individual hosts, not site-wide, and the RFC leaves failure detection to RFC 5534.

today: RFC 5533 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Failure detection and locator pair exploration are defined in RFC 5534 and the address bindings in RFC 5535.

sections.title: The Multihoming Goal
sections.content:
RFC 5533 defines Shim6, a layer 3 shim that provides locator agility below the transport protocols. It gives IPv6 multihoming with failover and load-sharing, without assuming that a multihomed site has a provider-independent prefix in the global IPv6 routing table. Hosts in a site with several provider-allocated prefixes use Shim6 to set up state with peers, so they can later fail over to a different locator pair if the original one stops working.

The goals include preserving established communication such as TCP connections and UDP streams, having minimal impact on upper layers, and not requiring an extra round trip up front: ULP traffic flows as normal and shim state is set up after some packets have been exchanged. The RFC uses the term load spreading rather than load balancing, since load may be spread unevenly.

Explicit non-goals: making communication survive a renumbering event, solving host mobility, and creating a new identifier name space. Shim6 processing happens in individual hosts, not through site-wide mechanisms.
sections.eli5: If a family has two roads into their house, a helper makes sure a visit can switch roads if one gets blocked. The helper lives in each computer, not in the neighborhood.

sections.title: Locators, ULIDs and Contexts
sections.content:
Shim6 splits the two jobs of an IPv6 address. A locator is the address as the network uses it for routing and forwarding. An upper-layer identifier (ULID) is the address the upper layer uses, for example in pseudo-header checksums and connection identification. No new name space is created: the ULID is just the locator picked at initial contact, chosen with default address selection from RFC 3484.

The shim keeps a ULID-pair context per pair of ULIDs, roughly per peer host and independent of individual connections. Each end allocates a Context Tag, a 47-bit number, so that received control messages and payload headers can be matched to the context. A context also holds the peer's locator list, the current locator pair and timers. Each end has its own current locator pair, and the two may differ.

Context forking lets a Shim6-aware upper layer use more than one locator pair for the same ULID pair. A forked context gets a non-zero 32-bit Forked Instance Identifier (FII); the default context has FII zero.
sections.eli5: Your name tag stays the same all day, but you may enter the building through different doors. The name tag is the ULID and the doors are locators. A ticket number, the Context Tag, shows which conversation a message belongs to.

sections.title: Where the Shim Sits
sections.content:
The shim is inside the IP layer, below the upper-layer protocols. It sits between the IP endpoint sub-layer, which handles fragmentation, reassembly and destination options, and the IP routing sub-layer, which picks the next hop and interface. Putting fragmentation above the shim keeps reassembly robust if fragments take different paths with different source locators.

The sender maps ULIDs to locators and the receiver maps them back, so upper layers see packets that appear to use ULIDs end to end. As a result there is no impact on pseudo-header checksums or connection identification. The RFC suggests thinking of it as header compression: the ULIDs are not carried once state is set up, and a Context Tag tells the receiver which context to use to restore them.

IP multicast is deliberately left out. Multicast routing needs a topologically correct source address for the RPF check, so multicast upper layers operate directly on locators and do not use the shim.
sections.eli5: It is like a translator standing between your letter and the post office. You write the same address on every letter, and the translator swaps in a working address on the envelope. At the other end the translator swaps it back.

sections.title: From Initial Contact to Failover
sections.content:
At initial contact there is no shim action. Later, a heuristic on one or both hosts decides the overhead is worthwhile, for instance after more than 50 packets or a timer expiring during active exchange, and starts context establishment. If it fails, the initiator concludes the other end does not support Shim6 and carries on normally. While the ULID pair is also the locator pair, ULP packets carry no Shim6 header.

When something fails, one or both ends probe alternate locator pairs until one works, then switch. After a switch the sender rewrites the addresses and adds a Shim6 Payload Extension header holding the receiver's Context Tag. If the original ULIDs become the active pair again, the header is no longer needed. A host that knows a locator is unusable, such as an interface that went down, can tell its peer, and preferences can also be signalled with a Locator Preferences option.

State can be garbage collected without coordinating with the peer. A recovery message reports missing context, which handles both premature cleanup and a peer crash. Detection of failure and the search for a working pair are specified in RFC 5534, and this document only reserves its message types.
sections.eli5: Everything works normally until a road is blocked. Then the helper tries the other roads, finds one that works, and puts a small tag on each letter so the other side knows which conversation it belongs to.

sections.title: Shim6 Messages and Headers
sections.content:
All Shim6 messages use IP protocol number 140 and are structured as an IPv6 extension header, so one protocol number has to be allowed through firewalls. The first 17 bits are common: Next Header, Hdr Ext Len and a P bit. P is one for the Payload Extension header and zero for control messages. Signaling packets may not exceed 1280 bytes including the IPv6 header.

The Payload Extension header is 8 octets: Next Header, Hdr Ext Len of 0, the P bit set to one, and a 47-bit Receiver Context Tag. Control messages add a 7-bit Type, a checksum and type-specific fields. Their Next Header is normally NO_NXT_HDR (59), and the checksum has no pseudo-header, which provides locator agility without changing the checksum. Type codes 0-63 do not trigger R1bis on a missing context, while 64-127 do.

Options follow the fixed fields. The defined options include Responder Validator, Locator List, Locator Preferences, CGA Parameter Data Structure, CGA Signature, ULID Pair, Forked Instance Identifier and Keepalive Timeout.
sections.eli5: Each Shim6 message has a small header at the front, like a label on a parcel. A one-bit flag says whether the parcel carries ordinary data or a note between the two helpers.

sections.title: Setting Up and Recovering a Context
sections.content:
A context is normally established with a four-message exchange: I1 and R1, then I2 and R2. The responder keeps no state after I1; the R1 carries a Responder Validator and nonce that the initiator must return in I2. Each end allocates a Context Tag and shares its locator set. The tag MUST be unique among a host's contexts, and if an implementation structures tags, at least 30 bits MUST be unstructured random bits.

Crossing I1 messages from both sides are answered with an immediate R2. To recover a lost context, an R1bis is sent when a Shim6 control or payload header arrives with no matching context, and the peer answers with I2bis, followed by R2. Retransmission timers use binary exponential backoff randomized between 0.5 and 1.5 times the nominal value. I1 is retried up to I1_RETRIES_MAX (4) times with a 4-second timeout, after which the host assumes the peer lacks Shim6 and may remember that for at most one minute.

Locators must be verified. A host checks that a locator is bound to the ULID using HBA or CGA, and before using a locator as a destination it MUST also confirm the ULID is present there through a reachability probe. Update Request and Update Acknowledgement messages change the locator list later. ICMP errors that Shim6 can act on, such as Destination Unreachable codes 0, 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6, are handled by the shim; others, such as Packet Too Big, go to the upper layer.
sections.eli5: Two helpers introduce themselves in four short steps and swap lists of their addresses. The first one to speak does not make the other remember anything until it proves it is real.

sections.title: Security and IPsec
sections.content:
Redirection attacks are addressed with Hash-Based Addresses (HBA) or Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA), which bind the alternative locators to the original address. With CGA, RSA keys used for generation MUST be at least 1024 bits. Third-party flooding is prevented by requiring a successful reachability probe and reply before a new locator is used as a destination.

The first message creates no state on the responder, so a three-way exchange is needed before state is created, which limits memory-exhaustion attacks. Nonces defend against replay and off-path interference, and every control message after establishment carries the Context Tag, so an attacker generally needs to be on the path to spoof one. The RFC lists residual threats, including R1bis abuse and guessing of the 47-bit tag.

When the locator pair differs from the ULID pair, Shim6 behaves conceptually like a tunnel with a compressed inner header, so interaction with IPsec resembles IPsec with tunnels, and IPsec can be seen as applied both above and below the shim. Middle-boxes that check upper-layer validity using the IPv6 header addresses may fail on Shim6 payload packets, and the RFC recommends they not drop such packets.
sections.eli5: Only the true owner of an address can prove that a new address belongs to the same conversation, and the helper checks that first. A secret ticket number makes it hard for a stranger to butt in.
